↳ Posted by JACKB on February 16th, 2014.

. The name ‘Corney is coming’.

‘Gorrie is Coming’ (Thanig Gorrie) is the name of a pibroch recorded by a piper named Campbell in his collecttion, The Nether Lorne MS, around the end of the 18th century. It is a totally different tune, but the title echoes a song from Man about King Gorrie (Godfrey) who tried three times to invade and conquer the island, before succeeding. He died around 1098AD, and a branch of his descendants are known as ‘Siol Gorrie’ (The Seed of Godfrey), the MacDonalds of Sleat. Runrig recorded a song of this name. So the title may be much older than these tales suggest

↳ Posted by siubhal on February 16th, 2014.

↳ Posted by William Beers on August 9th, 2019.

Re: Corney Is Coming

Ceol Rince na hÉireann Vol.3, although it doesn’t say exactly where the name came from.

The notes say, “ Tá Cornaí ag Teacht: Corney is Coming [ditto in O’Neill, DMI 762, MI 1548]. Willie Clancy, 1/B/9(b). The Bride to Bed, Brides to Bed, My Love is in America in Goodman (G I, p52, G III, p106, and G IV, p89 respectively). Joyce changed the second name to Brides Away. My Love in the House is his name for another version (J, iii, p252). First printed by Bremner as Knit the Pocky (Coll. of Scots Reels, etc., 1751-61). Other names for it are The British Naggon, Merry Bits of Timber, Shannon Breeze, Cheese It, I Saw Her, The Barrack St. Boys, Miss Wilson, Kelly’s Reel, Crawford’s Reel, The Honeymoon and Six Mile Bridge.”

Re: Corney Is Coming

I heard that a man named Corney Drew lived in the Sliabh Luachra area in Kerry in the mid 19th Century and survived the Famine.
He passed on his traditional music to Tadhg Buckley aka Tadghin An Asail.
Tadhg in turn taught Tom Billy Murphy who later passed the tunes to Padraig O’ Keeffe.
The Padraig O’Keeffe Festival is held the last weekend of October each year in Castleisland.
So maybe it was a fairly common name in our history ….!?
